claim: T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) and k-means clustering identified 22 immune cell populations in the PB and synovial fluid (SF) compartments.
source: T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) and k-means clustering identified 22 immune cell populations in the PB and synovial fluid (SF) compartments (Figure 1A, p<1e−21, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CyTOF analysis and statistical significance (p<1e−21), and references to figures showing the results.

claim: These populations could be broadly segregated into Treg (CD25+/FoxP3+), naive (CD45RA+), effector/memory (CD45RA-), and non-T cell populations (CD3−/CD4−/CD8−).
source: These populations could be broadly segregated into Treg (CD25+/FoxP3+), naive (CD45RA+), effector/memory (CD45RA-), and non-T cell populations (CD3−/CD4−/CD8−).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis and classification of immune cell populations identified in the study.

claim: Preliminary clustering of the median marker expression on T cells revealed a clear demarcation of SFMCs and PBMCs.
source: Preliminary clustering of the median marker expression on T cells revealed a clear demarcation of SFMCs and PBMCs (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a strong association of immune phenotypes between intra-individual paired knee SFMCs.
source: Preliminary clustering of the median marker expression on T cells revealed a clear demarcation of SFMCs and PBMCs (Figure 1B), and a strong association of immune phenotypes between intra-individual paired knee SFMCs.
evidence: The claim is based on clustering analysis comparing immune phenotypes between paired knee samples.

claim: Density maps of immune cell populations within the t-SNE indicate strong dichotomy in the locations of SFMC and PBMC subsets.
source: Furthermore, density maps of immune cell populations within the t-SNE indicate strong dichotomy in the locations of SFMC and PBMC subsets (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by density map visualization shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SMFCs were enriched in CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ Tregs (node 2), and CD4+CD45RA− memory T cells (nodes 5, 9, and 10).
source: Comparison of the node fingerprints between SFMC and PBMC samples (Figure 1D) revealed that SMFCs were enriched in CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ Tregs (node 2), and CD4+CD45RA− memory T cells (nodes 5, 9, and 10)
evidence: The claim is supported by node fingerprint analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PBMCs were enriched in CD45RA+ naive T cells (nodes 3, 6, 7, 13, and 15).
source: while PBMCs were enriched in CD45RA+ naive T cells (nodes 3, 6, 7, 13, and 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by node fingerprint analysis.

claim: A strikingly similar cellular distribution profile was observed in the left and right knee joints of each JIA individual.
source: Next to this, a strikingly similar cellular distribution profile was observed in the left and right knee joints of each JIA individual (Figure 1C/D).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of cellular distribution profiles in Figure 1C/D.

claim: The correlation matrix of the entire spectrum of node frequencies demonstrated a strong positive correlation between the SFMCs and their left and right joints.
source: The correlation matrix of the entire spectrum of node frequencies demonstrated a strong positive correlation between the SFMCs and their left and right joints, and a strong negative correlation compared with the PBMC populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between SFMCs and PBMC populations.
source: The correlation matrix of the entire spectrum of node frequencies demonstrated a strong positive correlation between the SFMCs and their left and right joints, and a strong negative correlation compared with the PBMC populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: While distinct differences in T cell signatures can be identified between PB and SF compartments, the phenotypic T cell architecture of distinct inflamed sites (left and right knees) are remarkably similar.
source: These results demonstrate that, while distinct differences in T cell signatures can be identified between PB and SF compartments, the phenotypic T cell architecture of distinct inflamed sites (left and right knees) are remarkably similar, indicating commonality in underlying disease etiology.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of T cell signatures across different compartments and sites.

claim: The similarity in T cell architecture between distinct inflamed sites indicates commonality in underlying disease etiology.
source: These results demonstrate that, while distinct differences in T cell signatures can be identified between PB and SF compartments, the phenotypic T cell architecture of distinct inflamed sites (left and right knees) are remarkably similar, indicating commonality in underlying disease etiology.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observed similarity in T cell architecture.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets displayed an increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IFNγ, and IL-6).
source: Next, we functionally characterized SFMC-specific T cells, and found that CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets displayed an increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IFNγ, and IL-6), indications of chronic TCR activation (PD1 and LAG3) (Petrelli et al., 2018) and a memory phenotype (CD45RA−), compared to their PBMC counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional characterization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets displayed indications of chronic TCR activation (PD1 and LAG3).
source: Next, we functionally characterized SFMC-specific T cells, and found that CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets displayed an increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IFNγ, and IL-6), indications of chronic TCR activation (PD1 and LAG3) (Petrelli et al., 2018) and a memory phenotype (CD45RA−), compared to their PBMC counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional characterization data and citation to previous work (Petrelli et al., 2018).

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets displayed a memory phenotype (CD45RA−) compared to their PBMC counterparts.
source: Next, we functionally characterized SFMC-specific T cells, and found that CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets displayed an increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IFNγ, and IL-6), indications of chronic TCR activation (PD1 and LAG3) (Petrelli et al., 2018) and a memory phenotype (CD45RA−), compared to their PBMC counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional characterization data with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: The cytokine diversity of CD4+ memory T cells revealed nearly identical profiles for the left and right knee joints for each individual.
source: Remarkably, the cytokine diversity of CD4+ memory T cells revealed nearly identical profiles for the left and right knee joints for each individual (Figure 2A), with minor inter-individual differences.
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine profile analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There are minor inter-individual differences in cytokine profiles of CD4+ memory T cells.
source: Remarkably, the cytokine diversity of CD4+ memory T cells revealed nearly identical profiles for the left and right knee joints for each individual (Figure 2A), with minor inter-individual differences.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of cytokine profile data.

claim: The trend in cytokine profile was also reflected in the CD8+CD45RA− compartment.
source: This trend in cytokine profile was also reflected in the CD8+CD45RA− compartment (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis, though the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The Treg (CD25+FOXP3+) population was significantly enriched in SFMC.
source: The Treg (CD25+FOXP3+) population was significantly enriched in SFMC (Figure 2B, p<0.05, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: SFMC Tregs displayed enhanced expression of memory (CD45RA−) and activation markers (HLA-DR/ICOS).
source: The Treg (CD25+FOXP3+) population was significantly enriched in SFMC (Figure 2B, p<0.05, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D) with enhanced expression of memory (CD45RA−) and activation markers (HLA-DR/ICOS).
evidence: The claim is supported by marker expression analysis.

claim: SFMC memory Tregs displayed a significantly higher proliferation (Ki67) as compared to SFMC effector memory T cells.
source: Additionally, SFMC memory Tregs displayed a significantly higher proliferation (Ki67) as compared to SFMC effector memory T cells (Figure 2B, p<0.05), which was further confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation marker data with statistical significance (p<0.05) and confirmed by flow cytometry.

claim: Tregs belong to the most proliferative T cell subset in the inflamed environment.
source: This indicates that Tregs belong to the most proliferative T cell subset in the inflamed environment.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the Ki67 proliferation data.

claim: Memory Tregs showed very similar CTLA4/HLA-DR/ICOS/PD1 expression profiles in the left and right knee joints for each individual.
source: Moreover, memory Tregs showed very similar CTLA4/HLA-DR/ICOS/PD1 expression profiles in the left and right knee joints for each individual (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by marker expression profile data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Within JIA patients, there is an identical T cell phenotypic and functional profile present at separate inflamed locations.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that within JIA patients, there is an identical T cell phenotypic and functional profile present at separate inflamed locations, with increased amounts of activated and proliferating Treg populations.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the phenotypic and functional data presented.

claim: There are increased amounts of activated and proliferating Treg populations at inflamed locations in JIA patients.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that within JIA patients, there is an identical T cell phenotypic and functional profile present at separate inflamed locations, with increased amounts of activated and proliferating Treg populations.
evidence: The claim is based on the observed enrichment and proliferation data of Tregs.

claim: A cluster of CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs showed increased frequency in RA patients compared to OA.
source: We identified a cluster of CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs (characterized by high CD4, FOXP3, PDCD1, CTLA4, TIGIT, and IL2RA expression, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B) that showed increased frequency in RA patients compared to OA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell transcriptomics data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The increase of Tregs in RA SFMCs is consistent with the high frequency of Tregs observed in JIA SFMC samples.
source: This increase of Tregs in RA SFMCs is consistent with the high frequency of Tregs that we observed in our JIA SFMC samples (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is an inference comparing findings from RA data to JIA data.

claim: The expression of markers related to chronic TCR activation (PDCD1, CTLA4, and ICOS) were significantly increased in RA compared to OA.
source: Additionally, the expression of markers related to chronic TCR activation (PDCD1, CTLA4, and ICOS), and cytokines (TNF, IFNG, and GZMB) were significantly increased in RA compared to OA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), in line with what we observed in JIA SFMC (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The expression of cytokines (TNF, IFNG, and GZMB) were significantly increased in RA compared to OA.
source: Additionally, the expression of markers related to chronic TCR activation (PDCD1, CTLA4, and ICOS), and cytokines (TNF, IFNG, and GZMB) were significantly increased in RA compared to OA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), in line with what we observed in JIA SFMC (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The increased expression of activation markers and cytokines in RA is in line with what was observed in JIA SFMC.
source: Additionally, the expression of markers related to chronic TCR activation (PDCD1, CTLA4, and ICOS), and cytokines (TNF, IFNG, and GZMB) were significantly increased in RA compared to OA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), in line with what we observed in JIA SFMC (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: The claim is an inference comparing findings from RA data to JIA data.

claim: Within the inflamed joints, clonally expanded cells were detected, which was more pronounced for Tregs than non-Tregs.
source: Within the inflamed joints, clonally expanded cells were detected, which was more pronounced for Tregs than non-Tregs (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The distribution of T cell clones was highly similar between left and right joints, both for Tregs and non-Tregs.
source: In line with the CyTOF analysis, the distribution of T cell clones was highly similar between left and right joints, both for Tregs and non-Tregs.
evidence: The claim is based on TCR sequencing data analysis comparing clone distribution.

claim: There is a high degree of sharing of hyper-expanded T cells between two affected joints.
source: Hyper-expanded T cells were further studied by the sequential intersection of the most abundant TCRβ clonotypes across samples. We found a high degree of sharing between two affected joints, while a small fraction of clones was shared between SF and PB (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequential intersection analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A small fraction of clones was shared between SF and PB.
source: We found a high degree of sharing between two affected joints, while a small fraction of clones was shared between SF and PB (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequential intersection analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sharing of clones between two joints was more evident for Tregs than non-Tregs.
source: Moreover, sharing of clones between two joints was more evident for Tregs than non-Tregs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequential intersection analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Frequencies of hyper-expanded T cells were highly conserved between distinct anatomical sites.
source: Detailed analysis further revealed that frequencies of hyper-expanded T cells were highly conserved between distinct anatomical sites, with the most dominant clones also detectable in PB (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency plot analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The most dominant clones are also detectable in PB.
source: Detailed analysis further revealed that frequencies of hyper-expanded T cells were highly conserved between distinct anatomical sites, with the most dominant clones also detectable in PB (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency plot analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Frequencies of shared clones were not correlated with pgen.
source: Frequencies of shared clones were not correlated with pgen (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Frequencies of non-shared clones showed a significant positive correlation with pgen.
source: while frequencies of non-shared clones showed a significant positive correlation with pgen (Figure 3E).

claim: The correlation between frequency and pgen was more pronounced for non-Tregs.
source: Notably, this correlation was more pronounced for non-Tregs (Figure 3E), indicating either bystander activation or non-antigen-specific circulation of the non-shared TCR clones in the non-Treg compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The correlation between frequency and pgen for non-shared non-Treg clones indicates either bystander activation or non-antigen-specific circulation.
source: Notably, this correlation was more pronounced for non-Tregs (Figure 3E), indicating either bystander activation or non-antigen-specific circulation of the non-shared TCR clones in the non-Treg compartment.

claim: Both non-Treg and Treg hyper-expanded T cell clones are shared between inflamed joints.
source: In summary, both non-Treg and Treg hyper-expanded T cell clones are shared between inflamed joints.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the TCR sequencing data analysis.

claim: The overlap of hyper-expanded T cell clones is most pronounced for Treg.
source: This overlap is most pronounced for Treg, with the highly dominant Treg clones in SF also being detectable in circulation, likely driven by responses to shared antigens.

claim: The highly dominant Treg clones in SF are also detectable in circulation.
source: This overlap is most pronounced for Treg, with the highly dominant Treg clones in SF also being detectable in circulation, likely driven by responses to shared antigens.

claim: The sharing of dominant Treg clones is likely driven by responses to shared antigens.
source: This overlap is most pronounced for Treg, with the highly dominant Treg clones in SF also being detectable in circulation, likely driven by responses to shared antigens.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed clone sharing and lack of correlation with pgen.

claim: The estimated species richness and Shannon diversity was significantly lower for JIA Tregs compared to Tregs obtained from healthy donors.

claim: The JIA Treg repertoire is less diverse than healthy.

evidence: The claim is an inference based on the diversity analysis results.

claim: TCRβs of SF Tregs were highly shared within patients over time.
source: Repertoire overlap analysis showed that TCRβs of SF Tregs were highly shared within patients over time (Figure 4A), which was also conserved across different joints (Figure 4A/B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by repertoire overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TCRβ sharing of SF Tregs was also conserved across different joints.
source: Repertoire overlap analysis showed that TCRβs of SF Tregs were highly shared within patients over time (Figure 4A), which was also conserved across different joints (Figure 4A/B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).

claim: TCRβs from PB did not cluster together over time.

claim: TCRβs from PB showed much less overlap with their synovial counterparts.

claim: The most dominant T cell clones have the highest degree of sharing over time.

claim: Persistent TCRβs with high abundance were not driven by recombination bias.

claim: During relapsing-remitting disease, persistent dominant T cell clones are taking part in the local immune response in JIA patients.
source: Collectively, these data show that during relapsing-remitting disease, persistent dominant T cell clones are taking part in the local immune response in JIA patients, and this phenomenon is more pronounced for Tregs than non-Tregs.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the longitudinal TCR sequencing data.

claim: The phenomenon of persistent dominant T cell clones is more pronounced for Tregs than non-Tregs.

claim: Non-Tregs display sharing of TCRβ sequences over time.

claim: The degree of sharing of TCRβ sequences over time was less pronounced for non-Tregs compared to Tregs.

claim: Frequencies of highly shared TCRβs in non-Tregs were not driven by recombination bias.

claim: TCR networks from JIA patients were highly connected (more than expected by chance).

claim: TCRs from JIA samples display higher sequence similarity than expected by chance.

claim: The SF Treg repertoire is highly skewed by antigenic selection.

claim: Many autoimmune diseases are associated with the expression of specific MHC (HLA) class II alleles.
source: First, many autoimmune diseases are associated with the expression of specific MHC (HLA) class II alleles, which is hypothesized to lead to altered antigen presentation and enhanced CD4+ T cell activation (David et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (David et al., 2018).

claim: Specific MHC (HLA) class II alleles are hypothesized to lead to altered antigen presentation and enhanced CD4+ T cell activation.

claim: Tregs with a high degree of self-reactivity were found to be expanding locally in affected pancreatic islets in mice with type 1 diabetes.
source: Further support for the hypothesis that persistent, hyper-expanded Tregs found in JIA SF are auto-reactive is provided by a recent study performed in mice with type 1 diabetes, where Tregs with a high degree of self-reactivity were found to be expanding locally in affected pancreatic islets and displayed a specific profile with elevated levels of GITR, CTLA-4, ICOS, and Ki67, very similar to our observations (Sprouse et al., 2018).
